title: Molecule
summary: A molecule is two or more atoms held together by covalent bonds — the smallest unit of a substance that still keeps its identity. Explore how atoms team up to build molecules like water, oxygen, and methane.

compareCandidate.label: Molecule vs. compound
compareCandidate.description: A molecule is any two or more atoms bonded covalently — they can be the same element (O₂) or different (H₂O). A compound is a substance made of different elements bonded together. Every compound is made of molecules or ions; not every molecule is a compound.

parts: The smallest unit of a substance
processes: Acting as the smallest particle that keeps a substance's identity
Forming everything from air to proteins
plainLanguageExplanation: A molecule is simply a team of atoms joined by covalent bonds. Think of the air you breathe: the oxygen is not single atoms — it is pairs of oxygen atoms holding hands, O₂, each pair one molecule. Water is a slightly bigger team — two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom, H₂O, one molecule. The most important idea about molecules is that they are the smallest unit of a substance that still acts like that substance. Break a water molecule apart and you no longer have water — you have separate hydrogen and oxygen atoms. Molecules can be tiny, like O₂ with just two atoms, or enormous, like the DNA molecules inside your cells with millions of atoms. What makes something a molecule is simple: two or more atoms, joined by covalent bonds, acting as one unit. When those atoms are from different elements, the molecule is also a compound; when they are all the same element, like O₂, it is just that element in molecular form.

whyItMatters: Molecules are the smallest pieces of almost everything you can touch, drink, and breathe. Water, air, food, medicines, and the DNA inside you are all built from molecules. Knowing what a molecule is — and how its atoms team up — is the foundation for understanding compounds, chemical reactions, and how matter changes.
didYouKnow: A single drop of water holds roughly a billion trillion (10²¹) water molecules — every one of them exactly two hydrogens and one oxygen.
compareReason: The line between a molecule and a compound trips up every student — comparing O₂ with H₂O shows precisely where the two ideas split.
